ambition.rationale: The core problem is a forensic inverse problem: recover where and when a real fire started from sparse, late perimeters, with calibrated uncertainty and a rule that withholds the start time when the data cannot pin it. That is well beyond a familiar app with a model attached. The hard part is custom and non-LLM: a time-dependent Dijkstra spread engine, a two-stage search over origin, start time and spread scale, and simulation-based calibration against synthetic fires whose truth differs from the inverted model in kind. The LLM analyst and the debris-flow models are ordinary patterns (tool-calling with cite checks; stock random forests and MLPs), and the README admits the ML did not beat USGS's M1. The "not possible a year ago" claim is weakly supported: the 2025 fire data was public from early 2025 and the methods (Anderson 1983 ellipse, minimum-travel-time spread, Mantel-Haenszel) are decades old. The 2026 debris inventory and the combination are the newer parts. Score 7: clearly above ordinary, not yet at the frontier of novelty.

depth.rationale: The hard part is largely original, not glue. The spread model is a hand-written numba time-dependent Dijkstra with an elliptical rate of spread and slope-equivalent wind, not a library call. The ignition inversion searches a full stage-1 grid, takes its posterior from that grid only, calibrates the posterior temperature on half the synthetic cases and checks coverage on the other half, and withholds the start time under an identifiability gate. The debris work adds a within-storm ranking metric and a leave-one-fire-out design, and the exposure statistics (Mantel-Haenszel with RBG variance, IRLS logistic) are hand-written and match the standard formulas. Rough share: about 30 percent of the non-test Python (roughly 2,000 of 6,560 lines) is algorithmic; the rest is fetching, caching, parsing and UI wiring. The web 3D stage is mostly deck.gl composition with one hand-written shader module. The analyst tool loop is standard glue; its verifier is the custom part, but its number grounding is presence-based and the analyst has never been run live. Held to 8 by one free spread-rate scale plus a per-fire shape cap over ad hoc fuel constants, a synthetic benchmark partly tied to the real fit, default scikit-learn debris estimators, and thin calibration (15 unseen cases per scenario).
